## 1. Identification Strategy  
Difference-in-Differences (DID) augmented with an event–study (dynamic DID) at the individual-micro level.

Why this works  
• The Mariel boatlift was a large, sudden, plausibly exogenous shock confined to one city.  
• We observe repeated cross-sections before (1979-Apr 1980) and after (Oct 1980-1985) for Miami and several unaffected comparison cities.  
• DID compares the change in outcomes for Miami to the contemporaneous change in the control cities, differencing out common macro trends.  
• An event study of yearly leads/lags lets us test for pre-trends and trace dynamics.  
• Because outcomes are measured for individuals, we can add rich covariates and interact DID with skill group (low-skill natives, earlier Cubans, high-skill natives, etc.) to produce a “triple-difference” within the same framework.

## 2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment definition  
• Unit of observation: individual i in city c at time t.  
• Treated = (c = Miami) × (t ≥ Oct 1980).  
• We will further interact treatment with:  
 – Low-skill natives: U.S.–born, ≤ high-school, potential experience ≤ 20.  
 – Earlier Cubans: Foreign-born in Cuba, arrived ≤ 1979.  

Control group  
• Individuals in Atlanta, Houston, Los Angeles, and Tampa-St. Petersburg in the same months/years. These cities are chosen ex-ante for demographic and growth similarity but did not experience the refugee shock.

Treatment timing  
• Event date: Apr 1980 (Census reference day). We code the post-period starting with Oct 1980 CPS ORG wave to allow the boatlift to complete (May–Sep) and avoid contemporaneous measurement in flux months.  
• Pre-period: Jan 1979–Apr 1980.  
• Post-period: Oct 1980–Dec 1985. (We drop May–Sep 1980 as the transition.)

No RDD is contemplated; the running dimension is time and location, not a scalar forcing variable.

## 3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1 (Parallel trends). In the absence of the boatlift, labor-market outcomes for less-skilled Miami workers would have evolved like those in the comparison cities.  
 Plausibility: The chosen controls had similar 1970s wage/unemployment trajectories and industrial mix; event-study pre-coefficients will be examined.

A2 (No interference / SUTVA across cities). The boatlift did not appreciably affect wages or employment in the four comparison MSAs.  
 Plausibility: The refugees overwhelmingly settled in Miami; spatial frictions and contemporaneous size (≈ 1% of each control city’s labor force if evenly spread) suggest minimal spillovers.

A3 (Exogeneity of the shock). The timing and size of the Mariel inflow were driven by Cuban political decisions, not Miami labor demand.  
 Plausibility: Widely viewed as sudden and unanticipated; institutional history supports.

A4 (Stable composition). Any endogenous migration of natives or firms in response to the shock is small or captured by city×year fixed effects.  
 Plausibility: Short horizon limits large out-migration; we will test using CPS mobility questions.

## 4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  

1. Differential pre-trends.  
 Check: Graph event-study leads; run placebo DID on 1977–1979 only.  
 Fix: Re-weight control cities (synthetic control style) or interact controls with pre-trend.

2. Selective out-migration of natives from Miami post-1980.  
 Check: Use March CPS Mobility Supplement to track 5-year migration rates.  
 Fix: Estimate intent-to-treat (all individuals in Miami samples, not tracking movers) and bound estimates with Lee (2009) trimming if exit rates differ.

3. Other contemporaneous Miami shocks (e.g., early-1980s recession’s industry-specific hit).  
 Check: Add city-specific linear time trends and industry×year fixed effects; drop industries that collapsed nationally as robustness.

## 5. R Code Outline  

```r
# 0. Packages
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)   # fast high-dim FE regressions
library(modelsummary)

# 1. Load CPS ORG micro data (assumed CSVs stacked by month)
cps <- read_csv("cps_1979_1985.csv")

# 2. Keep working-age
cps <- cps %>% filter(age >= 16 & age <= 61)

# 3. City indicator
cps <- cps %>%
  mutate(city = case_when(
    metro == "Miami-Fort Lauderdale" ~ "Miami",
    metro %in% c("Atlanta", "Houston", "Los Angeles", "Tampa-St. Petersburg") ~ metro,
    TRUE ~ NA_character_)) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(city))

# 4. Post indicator (omit May–Sep 1980)
cps <- cps %>% 
  mutate(post = if_else(year > 1980 | (year == 1980 & month >= 10), 1, 0))

# 5. Skill groups
cps <- cps %>%
  mutate(low_skill_native = (nativity == "US-born" & educ <= 12 & exper <= 20),
         earlier_cuban    = (birthplace == "Cuba" & arrival_year <= 1979))

# 6. Outcomes
cps <- cps %>%
  mutate(ln_wage      = log(hourly_earnings_CPI),
         unemployed   = as.integer(lfs == "Unemployed"),
         employed     = as.integer(lfs == "Employed"),
         in_lf        = as.integer(lfs != "Not in labor force"))

# 7. DID core – low-skill natives
did_native <- feols(ln_wage ~ post*Miami | city^month + educ + exper + female + race,
                    data = filter(cps, low_skill_native == TRUE & !is.na(ln_wage)),
                    cluster = ~city)

# 8. Triple-DID – earlier Cubans vs other Hispanics
cps <- cps %>%
  mutate(cuban_pre80 = if_else(earlier_cuban, 1, 0))

triple <- feols(ln_wage ~ post*Miami*cuban_pre80 | city^month + educ + exper + female,
                data = filter(cps, hispanic == 1 & !is.na(ln_wage)),
                cluster = ~city)

# 9. Event study (year dummies interacted with Miami)
cps <- cps %>% mutate(year_fe = factor(year))
event <- feols(ln_wage ~ i(year, Miami, ref = 1980) | city + month + educ + exper + female,
               data = filter(cps, low_skill_native == TRUE),
               cluster = ~city)

# 10. Robustness: synthetic weights
# (simplified illustration; actual synth requires more code)
# Create weights equalizing 1979 means of ln_wage
pre_means <- cps %>% filter(year == 1979) %>%
  group_by(city) %>% summarise(pre_w = mean(ln_wage, na.rm = TRUE))
cps <- cps %>% left_join(pre_means, by = "city") %>%
  mutate(weight = pre_w / pre_w[city == "Miami"])

did_weighted <- feols(ln_wage ~ post*Miami | city^month + educ + exper + female + race,
                      data = filter(cps, low_skill_native == TRUE),
                      weights = ~weight,
                      cluster = ~city)
```

Interpretation of coefficients  
• In `did_native`, the coefficient on `post:Miami` is the DID estimate of the log-wage effect (≈ %Δ).  
• In `triple`, the three-way interaction gives the differential impact on earlier Cubans relative to other Hispanics in control cities.

## 6. Expected Results  

Economic theory (simple competitive model) predicts:  
• A 7 % supply increase of low-skill workers should lower their wages unless labor demand is highly elastic; magnitude depends on σ (elasticity of substitution).  
• If σ ≈ 2, wage decline ≈ (ΔL/L)/(σ) ≈ 0.07/2 = -3.5 %.  
• Unemployment may rise 0–1 pp for very low-skill natives.  
• Earlier Cuban immigrants, who are closer substitutes, should experience equal or slightly larger negative effects (-4 % to ‑6 %).  
Overall, I expect small negative wage changes (-2 % to ‑5 %) and little change in unemployment because of Miami’s rapid growth and industrial flexibility.

## 7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)

C1 Clear treatment assignment (Miami vs controls): 1  
C2 No differential pre-trends: 0.5 (must be tested)  
C3 No spillovers to control units: 0.5  
C4 No other simultaneous shocks differentially hitting Miami: 0.5  
C5 Stable sample composition / no selective migration: 0.5  

Total: 3/5 → Moderately credible, contingent on passing pre-trend and mobility tests.
